section_summary: This section documents postwar efforts to restore Allied patent rights in Japan and permit Japanese nationals to seek patents abroad. It includes SCAP directives, Far Eastern Commission policy and press releases, diplomatic replies about Japanese applications, and discussion of an international accord on Japanese-owned patents outside Japan. The final pages raise questions about patent royalties and claims by the Sperry Corporation.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about a new synthesis of acrylic acid
subfiles.from: Mr. Nagataki, Toa Gosei Chemical Industry Company
subfiles.about: Asks whether a synthesis disclosed from captured German material is protected by patents and how it might be licensed.
subfiles.summary: The company seeks patent and royalty guidance before using the process in Japan.

subfiles.title: Instructions for reply to Toa Gosei Chemical Industry Company
subfiles.to: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Sets out the Department's response to Nagataki's patent inquiry.
subfiles.summary: The particular patents cannot be identified from the inquiry. German patents seized in Allied countries are governed by differing national rules and the London Patent Accord; German-owned patents in Japan remain in SCAP custody.

subfiles.title: Supplementary information on restoration procedures
subfiles.from: Office of the United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Transmits SCAPIN 1990/1 on restoration of Allied patent property in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Encloses supplementary restoration procedures for patents, utility models, and designs.

subfiles.title: SCAPIN 1990/1: Procedures for Restoration of Patent Property in Japan to Allied Nationals
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Directs procedures for investigating and restoring Allied-owned patents, utility models, and designs.
subfiles.summary: The Board of Patents is to report status, use, and royalties, record restoration and extensions, and issue certificates showing expiration dates and future fees.

subfiles.title: Comments on policy for Japanese patents outside Japan
subfiles.from: David L. Bazelon, Office of Alien Property
subfiles.about: Comments on a draft policy for former Japanese-owned patents outside Japan.
subfiles.summary: Bazelon supports its general approach but objects to eliminating the nominal licensing charge and failing to protect neutral and other non-enemy licensees. He proposes language based on the London Patent Accord.

subfiles.title: Final Act and Annexed Accord on German-Owned Patents
subfiles.from: London conference of governments represented in the Inter-Allied Reparation Agency
subfiles.about: Records the conference and sets terms for making former German-owned patents available among participating countries.
subfiles.summary: The Final Act identifies delegates, resolutions, and positions on sharing German technical information. The annexed accord calls for public dedication or royalty-free licensing of certain former German-owned patents, reciprocal access for nationals of signatory governments, protection of existing non-German interests, exchange of patent information, and procedures for signature and territorial extension.

subfiles.title: Reply accepting Office of Alien Property comments
subfiles.about: Acknowledges comments on the Japanese patents policy draft.
subfiles.summary: Brown says the draft will be revised before presentation to other countries.

subfiles.title: Swiss note on restoration of patent rights in Japan
subfiles.about: Asks that Swiss owners who lost Japanese patent rights during the war receive the restoration benefits granted to Allied nationals.
subfiles.summary: Switzerland argues its patent holders could have suffered comparable losses and asks that they not be excluded.

subfiles.title: Reply to Switzerland on Japanese patent rights
subfiles.about: Explains why the Allied restoration policy does not expressly cover Swiss nationals.
subfiles.summary: The policy addresses losses caused by enemy-property treatment or hostilities. Swiss claimants may seek relief in Japanese courts; Switzerland may raise inadequate remedies with SCAP through its Tokyo mission.

subfiles.title: Earlier draft reply to Swiss note
subfiles.about: Drafts a response concerning Swiss losses of patent rights in Japan.
subfiles.summary: This draft suggests supplying details to the Far Eastern Commission and seeking ordinary remedies in Japanese courts.

subfiles.title: Extension of priority time for patent applications in Japan
subfiles.about: Announces an interim directive extending patent application priority rights for nationals of countries at war with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Eligible applicants receive a twelve-month filing period after direct applications again become possible. Good-faith prior users may continue under nonexclusive licenses with reasonable royalties.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Commission policy toward patents, utility models, and designs in Japan
subfiles.about: Publishes the Commission's March 17 policy decision on Japanese industrial property.
subfiles.summary: The policy restores ordinary Patent Office functions, requires publication of secret patents, protects existing rights subject to occupation needs, and provides for restoration, extension, and reinstatement of Allied-owned patents and applications. It also covers registered utility models and designs.

subfiles.title: Additional information on Far Eastern Commission patent decision
subfiles.about: Explains the general and Allied-owner provisions of the patent policy.
subfiles.summary: The paper describes resumed publication and disclosure by the Japanese Patent Office, limits arising from occupation policy, and Allied owners' choice between restored royalties and an extension of patent duration.

subfiles.title: Japanese nationals permitted to file patents abroad
subfiles.from: Office of the United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Reports SCAP authorization and early Japanese interest in foreign patent filings.
subfiles.summary: Two applicants had approval to file five United States applications. A Japanese Patent Agency official describes strong interest in United States filings but notes restrictions concerning invention dates, potential use, travel, and fees.

subfiles.title: SCAPIN 2010: Patent Applications
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Sets conditions for Japanese nationals to file patent applications in foreign countries.
subfiles.summary: Applications require SCAP approval and ordinarily must concern inventions made after January 1, 1946 with potential foreign use. The directive regulates fees, foreign exchange, later patent transactions, and reporting.

subfiles.title: United States Patent Office forwarding letter
subfiles.about: Forwards a reply for the Japanese Board of Patents.
subfiles.summary: Forwards an answer about United States patents, designs, and trade marks.

subfiles.title: Instruction forwarding United States patent materials
subfiles.to: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Requests transmission of the Patent Office reply and patent law materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Encloses the Patent Office letter and two copies of United States patent laws and rules.

subfiles.title: Austrian letter for Japanese Board of Patents
subfiles.about: Transmits an Austrian ministry letter and enclosures for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Forwards an Austrian reply addressed to the Japanese Board of Patents.

subfiles.title: Swiss patent cancellation in SCAP report
subfiles.about: Notes a possible basis for Switzerland's protest over patent restoration policy.
subfiles.summary: A 1946 SCAP report lists one Swiss patent cancelled for nonpayment of fees.

subfiles.title: Czechoslovak position on Japanese patent applications
subfiles.about: Forwards Czechoslovakia's response concerning Japanese patents and trade marks.
subfiles.summary: Encloses three copies of the Czechoslovak Foreign Ministry note.

subfiles.title: Czechoslovak Foreign Ministry note, first translation
subfiles.about: States Czechoslovakia's treatment of Japanese patent, trade-mark, and sample applications.
subfiles.summary: Czechoslovakia regards the wartime suspension of the Paris Convention as continuing until a peace treaty. It is not processing Japanese patent applications or recognizing Japanese trade-mark and sample protection.

subfiles.title: Czechoslovak Foreign Ministry note, clean translation
subfiles.about: Provides a second translation of the Czechoslovak position.
subfiles.summary: Repeats that Japanese patents, trade marks, and samples lack protection pending a peace treaty.

subfiles.title: Instruction forwarding Czechoslovak note
subfiles.to: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Requests forwarding the Czechoslovak note to the Japanese Government.
subfiles.summary: Encloses Prague despatch No. 486 and the Czechoslovak ministry note.

subfiles.title: Routing note on Japanese patents policy
subfiles.about: Forwards a memorandum and proposed concurrence.
subfiles.summary: Says the attached proposal appears acceptable and includes a concurrence draft.

subfiles.title: Disposition of Japanese-owned patents outside Japan
subfiles.about: Proposes discussions outside the Far Eastern Commission after Soviet dissent blocked the patent policy.
subfiles.summary: The revised policy incorporates Office of Alien Property suggestions. Dixon proposes an informal meeting with supportive Far Eastern Commission delegates before seeking a wider international accord.

subfiles.title: Revised policy on Japanese patents outside Japan
subfiles.about: Sets proposed treatment of former Japanese-owned patents outside Japan.
subfiles.summary: Calls for public access while protecting non-enemy rights, publishing wartime applications, and accepting eligible post-1946 Japanese inventions.

subfiles.title: Swiss acknowledgement of State Department reply
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the August 11 reply on Japanese patent restoration.
subfiles.summary: The Swiss legation has sent the reply to authorities in Switzerland.

subfiles.title: Beirut despatch transmitting Lebanese reply
subfiles.about: Transmits a Lebanese reply concerning protection of Japanese industrial property.
subfiles.summary: Cover despatch for the Lebanese note; most text is illegible.

subfiles.title: Lebanese Foreign Ministry note, French copy
subfiles.about: Original-language note on protection of Japanese property.
subfiles.summary: The French text is largely illegible in the supplied OCR.

subfiles.title: Lebanese Foreign Ministry note, translation
subfiles.about: States that Lebanon sees no objection to protecting Japanese commercial and industrial property.
subfiles.summary: Lebanon's industrial property office raises no objection to granting protection.

subfiles.title: Instruction forwarding Lebanese note
subfiles.to: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Requests forwarding Lebanon's reply to the Japanese Government.
subfiles.summary: Encloses the Beirut despatch and Lebanese note with translation.

subfiles.title: Invitation to discuss Japanese patents outside Japan
subfiles.to: Harry Bullock and other embassy representatives
subfiles.about: Invites delegates to an October 5 meeting on an international arrangement for Japanese-owned patents abroad.
subfiles.summary: Explains that Soviet dissent prevented Far Eastern Commission adoption and encloses a revised policy aligned with the London Patent Accord.

subfiles.title: Amendment to restoration procedures
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Reports SCAPIN 1990/2 and a Japanese cabinet order on restitution of Allied patent property.
subfiles.summary: The amendment starts a one-year application period on September 1, 1949. The despatch also forwards a press release on Japan's implementing cabinet order and promises an official English translation.

subfiles.title: SCAPIN 1990/2: Restoration deadline amendment
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Amends the starting date in SCAPIN 1990.
subfiles.summary: Changes the restoration application period's starting date to September 1, 1949.

subfiles.title: Cabinet order on restitution of patent property
subfiles.about: Announces Japanese legislation restoring Allied-owned industrial property rights.
subfiles.summary: Describes revalidation, term extensions, fee relief, and priority claims under the new cabinet order.

subfiles.title: Translation of Cabinet Order No. 309
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Transmits an unofficial translation of Japan's industrial property restoration order.
subfiles.summary: Encloses K. Yuasa's translation and promises the official version when published.

subfiles.title: Questions about Cabinet Order No. 309
subfiles.to: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Requests clarification of possible differences between Japan's cabinet order and Far Eastern Commission policy.
subfiles.summary: Questions concern the definition of Allied nationals, wording on lapse or cancellation, restoration fees, third-party licenses, and coverage of utility models and designs. The Department suggests translation difficulties may explain them.

subfiles.title: Follow-up airgram on patent and trade-mark legislation
subfiles.about: Requests a prompt reply and identification of Japanese implementing legislation.
subfiles.summary: Seeks information on secret patents and laws implementing SCAPIN 2042 on trade marks.

subfiles.title: SCAP request for policy clarification
subfiles.to: Department of the Army for Joint Chiefs of Staff
subfiles.about: Asks whether policies cover patents and trade marks held by Japanese corporations with Allied ownership.
subfiles.summary: SCAP asks about rights lost under Japanese wartime custodianship and patents that expired during that period.

subfiles.title: Interim response to SCAP clarification request
subfiles.about: Advises that the State Department is preparing an interpretation of the patent policy.
subfiles.summary: A response to SCAP's questions is expected around November 5.

subfiles.title: Draft cable interpreting restoration policy
subfiles.about: Drafts an answer on Allied interests in patents and trade marks held by Japanese companies.
subfiles.summary: Restoration depends on enemy-property treatment, regardless of the extent of Allied ownership. Expired patents receive only their unexpired term at sequestration.

subfiles.title: Sperry Corporation inquiry about Japanese patents and royalties
subfiles.to: Department of State, Division of Economic and Property Policy
subfiles.about: Asks how Sperry Corporation can pursue Japanese patent and royalty claims.
subfiles.summary: Counsel asks whether procedures for wartime monetary claims have been established and whether specific claim forms are required.

subfiles.title: Draft reply to Sperry Corporation counsel
subfiles.about: Explains restoration and royalty options for Allied patent owners in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The reply describes the one-year application period beginning September 1, 1949, patent term extensions, and the required waiver of wartime royalty claims. It continues beyond this section.
